# Brain tumors

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Neurosurgery > Brain tumors*

[Original Article Link](/library/H50Klg)

---

## Summary

<u>Brain</u> tumors are masses of abnormal cells within the <u>brain</u>. They can be primary or <u>metastatic</u>, benign or malignant. Common tumors in children are pilocytic <u>astrocytomas</u>, <u>medulloblastomas</u>, <u>ependymomas</u>, and <u>craniopharyngiomas</u>. The most <u>common brain tumors in adults</u> are <u>glioblastomas</u>, <u>meningiomas</u>, <u>hemangioblastomas</u>, schwannomas, <u>oligodendrogliomas</u>, and <u>pituitary adenomas</u>. Clinical features and radiological findings vary according to the type, location, and onset of the <u>tumor</u>. <u>Magnetic resonance imaging</u> (<u>MRI</u>) is the primary diagnostic method. The histological <u>grade of the tumor</u> is an important factor in determining the prognosis. Removal of the entire <u>tumor</u> is a prerequisite for remission. <u>Malignant tumors</u> usually require additional treatment with <u>radiotherapy</u> and/or <u>chemotherapy</u>.




<u>Meningiomas</u>, <u>pituitary adenomas</u>, schwannomas, and <u>neoplastic meningitis</u> are discussed in separate articles.

---

## Epidemiology

* Approx. 30% of <u>brain</u> tumors are primary <u>brain</u> tumors, while approx. 70% are <u>metastases</u>.

* Approx. 40% of primary <u>brain</u> tumors are benign.

* Sex: <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u> (except <u>meningiomas</u>, which occur more frequently in women) [[1]](/library/BMXzIA)




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Approach

### Initial evaluation [[2]](/library/OL1IBh0)




#### Clinical assessment




* Obtain a thorough <u>patient history</u> and <u>neurological examination</u>.

* Suspect a <u>brain</u> <u>tumor</u> in patients with clinical features including:

* <u>Headaches</u> (especially with <u>headache red flags</u>)

* Other <u>signs of elevated intracranial pressure</u> (<u>ICP</u>), e.g., <u>papilledema</u>

* New onset <u>seizures</u>  [[3]](/library/x81EKi0)

* <u>Focal neurological deficits</u>;  depending on <u>tumor</u> location, e.g., sensory deficits

* <u>Nonfocal neurological deficits</u>

* Cognitive, behavioral, and <u>personality</u> changes





> [!TIP]
> Symptom onset in patients with primary <u>brain</u> tumors is usually insidious, while symptom onset in patients with <u>brain metastases</u> is typically acute or subacute.




#### Diagnostic testing




* Obtain <u>neuroimaging</u>.

* <u>Gadolinium</u>-enhanced <u>MRI</u> head: preferred

* CT head and neck with IV contrast: if <u>MRI</u> is not possible

* Further testing depends on imaging findings.

* Findings suggestive of primary <u>brain</u> <u>tumor</u>: Consult neurosurgery for diagnostic confirmation, e.g., via <u>brain biopsy</u> or resection

* Findings suggestive of <u>metastatic brain tumor</u>

* Initiate <u>diagnostics of cancer of unknown primary</u>.

* Obtain <u>biopsy</u> of the <u>brain metastasis</u> if primary is not identified. [[4]](/library/To16Y30)





### <u>Overview of MRI findings in brain tumors</u>




* There is significant overlap between <u>MRI</u> findings in common primary <u>brain</u> tumors (e.g., <u>gliomas</u>) and <u>brain metastases</u>.

* <u>Brain</u> tumors typically appear <u>hypointense</u> to <u>isointense</u> on <u>T1-weighted</u> images and <u>hyperintense</u> to <u>isointense</u> on <u>T2-weighted</u> images.





| Overview of MRI findings in brain tumors |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  |  | <u>MRI</u> findings |  |
| <u>Tumor</u> type |  |  | Typical location | Other findings |
| <br><u>Pilocytic astrocytoma</u> [[5]](/library/y81d6i0)<br> |  |  | <br>* <u>Cerebellum</u> or <u>optic nerve</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Intense, heterogeous <u>contrast enhancement</u> of solid portion; cyst wall typically non-enhancing<br><br>* Round or oval, well-demarcated, contrast-enhancing lesion within a larger, cystic lesion<br><br><br> |
| <br><u>Anaplastic astrocytoma</u> [[6]](/library/A81R6i0)<br> |  |  | <br>* Variable<br><br> | <br><br>* Nodular <u>enhancement</u> typically seen<br><br>* Heterogeneous lesion with perifocal <u>vasogenic edema</u><br><br>* No <u>necrosis</u> (in contrast to <u>glioblastoma</u>)<br><br><br> |
| <br><u>Glioblastoma multiforme</u> [[7]](/library/B81zKi0)<br> |  |  | <br>* Variable<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Contrast enhancement</u> usually present<br><br>* Localized multifocal garland-like <u>enhancements</u> with a <u>hypointense</u> <u>necrotic</u> core may be seen.<br><br><br> |

| <br><u>Meningioma</u> [[10]](/library/toXXd_)<br> |  |  | <br>* External surfaces of <u>brain</u>; within <u>ventricular system</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Homogeneous <u>enhancement</u><br><br>* Round, sharply demarcated lesions<br><br>* Thickened <u>dura mater</u><br><br><br> |
| <br><u>Metastasis</u> [[11]](/library/9K1Ni30)[[12]](/library/CK1qi30)[[13]](/library/C81qKi0)<br> |  |  | <br>* Gray-<u>white matter</u> junction and/or <u>watershed areas</u> of the arterial system; often, multiple nonlocalized lesions<br><br> | <br><br>* Well-circumscribed  <br><br>* Large <u>metastases</u>: <u>ring enhancement</u> due to central <u>necrosis</u><br><br>* Small <u>metastases</u>: homogeneous <u>enhancement</u><br><br>* More likely to be hemorrhagic than primary <u>brain</u> tumors<br><br>* <u>Edema</u> extensive relative to <u>tumor</u> size<br><br><br> |

### Management




### Principles of treatment




Management should be specialist guided; utilize a multidisciplinary approach and consult a <u>tumor board</u> if available.




* Management of <u>metastatic brain tumor</u>

* Identify and treat primary <u>malignancy</u>.

* See “<u>Brain metastases</u>” for details on treatment options.

* Management of primary <u>brain</u> <u>tumor</u>

* Based on both <u>tumor</u> and patient characteristics

* May include:

* Maximal safe surgical resection

* <u>Radiation therapy</u>: e.g., standard fractionated <u>external beam radiation therapy</u>

* Systemic therapy: e.g., <u>chemotherapy</u>, <u>cancer immunotherapy</u>

* Offer clinical trial enrollment and consider <u>palliative care</u> for patients with high-grade tumors (e.g., <u>glioblastoma multiforme</u>).





### Management of complications of brain tumors [[2]](/library/OL1IBh0)




See also ”<u>Cancer-related complications</u>” and “<u>Cancer treatment-related complications</u>.”




* <u>Venous thromboembolism</u> (<u>VTE</u>)  [[14]](/library/KlcUBc0)[[15]](/library/LL1wyh0)

* Consider <u>pharmacological VTE prophylaxis</u> for select patients.

* Offer therapeutic anticoagulation for patients with <u>VTE</u> (<u>LMWH</u> is the preferred agent).

* Patients with <u>brain</u> tumors are at increased risk of <u>intracerebral hemorrhage</u>; use <u>shared decision-making</u> for anticoagulation treatment decisions.

* <u>Seizures</u> [[16]](/library/ML1Myh0)[[17]](/library/nL17yh0)

* Primary prophylaxis is not recommended.

* Secondary prophylaxis (i.e., history of <u>seizures</u>): Initiate <u>treatment of epileptic seizures</u>.  [[18]](/library/-L1DZ30)

* <u>Vasogenic cerebral edema</u>

* Administer <u>glucocorticoids</u> (e.g., <u>dexamethasone</u> DOSAGE ) for patients with <u>signs of elevated ICP</u>. [[19]](/library/NL1-Bh0)[[20]](/library/8L1Ozh0)

* Follow local treatment protocols when available.





> [!WARNING]
> Certain types of <u>metastatic brain tumor</u> (e.g., <u>melanoma</u>, <u>renal cell carcinoma</u>) are more likely to hemorrhage, but are not an <u>absolute contraindication</u> to therapeutic anticoagulation. [[16]](/library/ML1Myh0)




> [!TIP]
> Taper and discontinue perioperative prophylactic medications within 7–10 days of <u>surgery</u>, unless otherwise indicated. [[2]](/library/OL1IBh0)

---

## Primary brain tumors

### Classification




Primary <u>brain</u> tumors arise within the <u>CNS</u> and are classified based on the growth characteristics and cell type from which the <u>tumor</u> arises.




#### By the spreading potential




| Types of <u>brain</u> tumors by growth characteristics |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | Low-grade brain tumors | High-grade brain tumors |
| WHO grade | I–II | III–IV |
| Borders | Well-defined | Poorly-defined |
| Spreading potential | Low | High |
| Recurrence | Rare | Frequent |





#### By <u>the cell</u> type




* <u>Gliomas</u> (e.g., <u>astrocytomas</u> and <u>oligodendrogliomas</u>)

* <u>Choroid plexus</u> tumors (e.g., <u>choroid plexus papilloma</u>, <u>choroid plexus carcinoma</u>)

* Neuronal and mixed neuronal-glial tumors (e.g., <u>paraganglioma</u>, <u>central neurocytoma</u>)

* <u>Meningiomas</u> (see “<u>Classification of meningiomas</u>”)

* Embryonal <u>neuroectodermal</u> tumors (e.g., <u>medulloblastoma</u>: , <u>CNS</u> <u>neuroblastoma</u>)

* <u>Pituitary tumors</u>: a group of tumors that arise from the <u>pituitary gland</u> (e.g., <u>pituitary adenoma</u>, <u>craniopharyngioma</u>)

* <u>Pineal tumors</u>

* Tumors of the <u>cranial</u> and paraspinal nerves (e.g., <u>schwannoma</u>: , <u>neuroma</u>, <u>neurofibroma</u>)

* <u>Mesenchymal</u> nonmeningeothelial tumors (e.g., <u>hemangiomas</u>, <u>hemangioblastoma</u>, <u>lipoma</u>, <u>hamartoma</u>)

* <u>Germ cell tumors</u> (e.g., <u>teratoma</u>)

* <u>Primary central nervous system lymphoma</u> (<u>PCNSL</u>)





### <u>Metastasis</u>




* Primary <u>CNS</u> tumors do not <u>metastasize</u> to organs outside the <u>CNS</u>.

* Drop metastases (intradural extramedullary spinal <u>metastases</u> ) and <u>leptomeningeal metastases</u> may occur. [[21]](/library/Qv0u-3)

* Typically manifest as <u>nodules</u> along the <u>spine</u> and <u>cauda equina</u> that can cause <u>back pain</u> with neurologic symptoms (e.g., limb <u>weakness</u>)

* Can be detected by <u>lumbar puncture</u>

---

## Astrocytoma

### Overview




<u>Astrocytomas</u> are neuroepithelial tumors (<u>gliomas</u>) that arise from <u>astrocytes</u>, which are a specific type of <u>glial cell</u>.




| Classification of astrocytomas |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Grade | Type | Description | <u>Epidemiology</u> | Location | Prognosis |
| I | <u>Pilocytic astrocytoma</u> | <br><br>* Slow growing, localized tumors<br><br>* Often associated with <u>neurofibromatosis type I</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Predominantly in children and young adults (< 20 years)<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Cerebellum</u> (most common)<br><br>* Cerebral hemispheres (<u>supratentorial</u>)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Favorable; long-term survival<br><br>* Completely curable with complete surgical resection<br><br>* Median survival: > 10 years<br><br><br> |
| II | <u>Diffuse astrocytoma</u> | <br>* Slow growing, low-grade <u>tumor</u> that has the potential to progress to higher-grade tumors<br><br> | <br>* Peak age: 20–40 years of age<br><br> | <br>* Cerebral hemisphere<br><br> | <br><br>* Incurable<br><br>* Median survival: 2–12 years<br><br><br> |
| III | <br><u>Anaplastic astrocytoma</u> [[22]](/library/-hYDgK)[[23]](/library/Z3YZSK)<br> | <br>* A slow-growing, infiltrative <u>tumor</u> that arises from <u>glial cells</u> in the <u>CNS</u><br><br> | <br>* Peak age: 30–50 years of age<br><br> | <br><br>* Incurable<br><br>* Median survival between 18 months and 10 years<br><br><br> |  |
| IV | <br><u>Glioblastoma multiforme</u> (<u>GBM</u>) [[24]](/library/Xv09A3)[[25]](/library/03YeSK)[[26]](/library/NqX-A_)<br> | <br>* <u>Malignant tumor</u> with rapid growth, abrupt symptom onset, and short disease course (<u>death</u> within weeks)<br><br> | <br><br>* Peak age: 60–70 years of age<br><br>* Most common malignant primary <u>brain</u> <u>tumor</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Cerebral <u>white matter</u><br><br>* Possibly bilateral: <u>butterfly glioma</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Incurable<br><br>* Median survival of 15 months<br><br><br> |

### Pilocytic astrocytoma [[27]](/library/Cv0qXR)[[28]](/library/xv0EXR)[[29]](/library/zhYrgK)[[30]](/library/fjYk-K)




* Description: slow-growing, circumscribed, non-invasive <u>tumor</u>

* <u>Epidemiology</u>

* Most commonly affects children and young adults (< 20 years)

* The most common primary <u>brain</u> <u>tumor</u> of childhood

* Associated conditions: <u>neurofibromatosis type I</u>

* Typical location

* <u>Cerebellum</u> (most common)

* Cerebral hemispheres (<u>supratentorial</u>)

* Clinical features

* Insidious onset and slow progression of symptoms

* <u>Vomiting</u>

* <u>Ataxia</u>

* <u>Failure to thrive</u>

* Diagnostics

* <u>MRI</u> findings

* Well-demarcated cystic lesion

* Bright contrast-enhancing solid <u>nodule</u> in the wall of the cyst

* <u>Histopathology</u>

* Microcysts

* Bipolar cells; <u>hair</u>-like projections

* Eosinophilic fibers with corkscrew appearance (<u>Rosenthal fibers</u>)

* Treatment: Surgical resection

* Prognosis

* Favorable prognosis: high rates of long-term survival

* Curable with complete resection of the <u>tumor</u>

* Median survival: > 10 years





![Cerebellar pilocytic astrocytoma](media/q36z4cv1y2t7zvenjl0lxnd3.jpg)

Cerebellar pilocytic astrocytoma




#### Optic glioma [[31]](/library/wv0hXR)




* Description

* Low-grade, slow-growing <u>tumor</u> that arises from the <u>glial cells</u> of the optic pathway

* Typically a grade I <u>pilocytic astrocytoma</u>

* <u>Epidemiology</u>: most frequently in children (< 10 years)

* Associated conditions: <u>neurofibromatosis type I</u>

* Clinical features

* Insidious onset and slow progression of symptoms

* <u>Proptosis</u>

* <u>Strabismus</u>

* Asymmetric <u>nystagmus</u>

* Impaired <u>vision</u> (in case of chiasmal involvement)

* Diagnostics

* <u>Fundoscopy</u> findings: retinal <u>pallor</u>, <u>papilledema</u>

* <u>MRI</u> findings: thickening of the <u>optic nerve</u> or <u>optic chiasm</u>; suprasellar mass

* Treatment

* No treatment in asymptomatic patients with no signs of <u>tumor</u> growth

* Surgical resection

* <u>Radiotherapy</u>

* Unresectable tumors, e.g., chiasmal or <u>optic tract</u> lesions in <u>optic glioma</u>

* Adjuvant to <u>surgery</u>

* Prognosis

* Favorable; high rates of long-term survival

* Many patients have long-term visual impairment.





### Diffuse astrocytoma




* Description: slow-growing, infiltrative <u>tumor</u> that arises from <u>glial cells</u> in the <u>CNS</u> and has the potential to progress to higher-grade tumors

* <u>Epidemiology</u>: peak age 20–40 years

* Location: cerebral hemispheres

* Clinical features

* Insidious onset and slow progression of symptoms

* Initially manifest with nonspecific features such as <u>headaches</u>, <u>seizures</u>

* Focal symptoms may develop (e.g, progressive <u>paralysis</u>, <u>aphasia</u>)

* Diagnostics

* CT: <u>hypodense</u> lesion with no <u>contrast enhancement</u>

* <u>MRI</u>

* T1 <u>hypointense</u> or <u>isointense</u>

* T2 <u>hyperintense</u>

* Treatment

* Complete surgical resection is often not possible. resection until definable margins can be attempted

* Percutaneous <u>radiotherapy</u> for very diffuse, unresectable tumors

* Prognosis: incurable; median survival: 2–12 years





### Anaplastic astrocytoma [[22]](/library/-hYDgK)[[23]](/library/Z3YZSK)




* Description: A high-grade infiltrative <u>tumor</u> with variable rates of growth that arises from <u>glial cells</u> in the <u>CNS</u>

* <u>Epidemiology</u>: peak age 30–50 years of age

* Clinical features

* <u>Headache</u>

* <u>Seizures</u>

* <u>Focal neurologic deficits</u>

* <u>Altered mental status</u>

* Diagnostics

* <u>MRI</u>

* Inhomogenous lesion with perifocal <u>edema</u>

* No <u>necrosis</u> (in contrast to <u>glioblastoma</u>)

* CT

* <u>Hypodense</u> lesion with variable <u>contrast enhancement</u>

* Positive <u>mass effect</u>

* Treatment

* <u>Tumor</u> <u>debulking</u> through <u>surgery</u>. However, complete surgical resection is not possible.

* Percutaneous <u>radiotherapy</u>/<u>chemotherapy</u>

* Prognosis: incurable; median survival between 18 months and 10 years





### Glioblastoma multiforme




* Description: : a highly <u>malignant tumor</u> derived from <u>glial cells</u> (e.g., <u>astrocytes</u>)

* <u>Epidemiology</u> [[32]](/library/eIXxbz)[[33]](/library/VIXGbz)[[34]](/library/gIXFXz)

* Most common <u>malignant brain tumor</u>

* Accounts for approx. 16% of all <u>CNS</u> <u>neoplasms</u>

* <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u> (1.6:1)

* Peak <u>incidence</u>: 64 years of age

* Primary <u>glioblastoma</u> (∼ 90%): more frequent in elderly patients (6<sup>th</sup> decade of life)

* Secondary <u>glioblastoma</u> (∼ 10%): affects primarily younger patients (4<sup>th</sup> decade of life)

* Etiology

* Environmental factors: <u>ionizing radiation</u>

* Genetic or <u>chromosomal</u> factors [[33]](/library/VIXGbz)

* Primary <u>glioblastoma</u>: arises de novo

* <u>EGFR</u> overexpression

* <u>PTEN gene</u> mutations [[35]](/library/UIXbXz)

* Loss of <u>chromosome</u> 10q

* Secondary <u>glioblastoma</u>: arises from a preexisting low-grade <u>tumor</u> (e.g., <u>diffuse astrocytoma</u>, <u>anaplastic astrocytoma</u>)

* <u>Isocitrate dehydrogenase</u> 1 (IDH1) mutations

* <u>p53</u> <u>gene mutations</u>

* Loss of <u>chromosome</u> 19q

* Associated conditions: rare occurrence of <u>glioblastoma</u> in patients with certain genetic syndromes (e.g., type I and II <u>neurofibromatosis</u>, <u>tuberous sclerosis</u>, <u>Li Fraumeni syndrome</u>, <u>Turcot syndrome</u>)

* Classification: The 2016 WHO classification groups <u>glioblastomas</u> mainly on the basis of <u>IDH</u> mutation status. [[36]](/library/4IX31z)

* <u>IDH</u>-wildtype <u>glioblastoma</u> (∼ 90%): usually corresponds with the clinically defined primary <u>glioblastoma</u>

* <u>IDH</u>-mutant <u>glioblastoma</u> (∼ 10%): usually corresponds with the clinically defined secondary <u>glioblastoma</u>

* Clinical features

* General clinical features of <u>brain</u> tumors (e.g., <u>signs of ↑ ICP</u>, <u>seizures</u>, <u>focal neurologic symptoms</u>)

* Short disease course with <u>death</u> within weeks (Rapid <u>tumor</u> growth)

* Apoplectic glioma: mimics <u>intracranial hemorrhage</u> and manifests with <u>signs of ↑ ICP</u>

* Typical location

* Primary <u>glioblastoma</u>

* <u>White matter</u> of the cerebral hemispheres (<u>supratentorial</u>)

* Possibly bilateral, crossing the corpus callosum: <u>butterfly glioma</u>

* Secondary <u>glioblastoma</u>: <u>frontal lobe</u>

* Diagnostics

* Characteristic features on <u>MRI</u> and CT

* Irregularly shaped, inhomogeneous mass

* Perifocal <u>vasogenic edema</u>

* <u>Mass effect</u>: midline shift, ventricular distortion

* Possibly hemorrhage

* <u>MRI</u> (<u>gadolinium</u>-enhanced)  

* Garland-like, enhanced margins with a <u>hypointense</u> <u>necrotic</u> core

* T1 <u>hypointense</u>

* T2 <u>hyperintense</u>

* May also have multifocal <u>enhancements</u>

* <u>Contrast-enhanced CT</u>: irregular, heterogeneous <u>enhancement</u> of the margins and <u>hypointense</u> center

* Evaluation of <u>IDH</u> mutation status (via <u>immunohistochemistry</u> or <u>genome</u> <u>sequencing</u>)

* <u>Biopsy</u>

* Dense, <u>pleomorphic</u> <u>anaplastic</u> cells that form pseudopalisades due to central <u>necrosis</u> or hemorrhage 

* A histopathologic finding characterized by elongated <u>nuclei</u> stacked in rows that often radiate away from a central area of <u>necrosis</u>

* Classically associated with <u>glioblastoma multiforme</u>

* <u>Microvascular</u> <u>proliferation</u>

* <u>GFAP</u> positive

* Treatment

* Surgical resection

* Palliative <u>radiochemotherapy</u> with <u>temozolomide</u>

* <u>Adjuvant chemotherapy</u> with <u>temozolomide</u>

* <u>Glucocorticoids</u>

* After recurrence

* Reresection, <u>temozolomide</u>, and/or radiation (if tolerated)

* The use of other <u>chemotherapeutic agents</u> (<u>carboplatin</u>, <u>etoposide</u>, <u>irinotecan</u>, <u>nitrosoureas</u>) can be tried as single agents or in regimens.

* <u>Bevacizumab</u>

* Tumor-treating fields (<u>TTFields</u>) [[37]](/library/FUcgUb0)

* Noninvasive treatment modality based on the transcutaneous delivery of alternating intermediate-frequency and low-intensity electric fields to disrupt <u>tumor</u> cell division and inhibit <u>tumor</u> growth

* The <u>electric field</u> interferes with cancer cells in a number of ways, including the alteration of <u>cell membrane</u> polarization and inhibition of <u>microtubule</u> polymerization.

* Can be given in combination with <u>adjuvant chemotherapy</u> (e.g., <u>temozolomide</u>)

* Prognosis [[33]](/library/VIXGbz)

* Median survival: 15 months

* Positive prognostic factors: <u>IDH</u>-mutant <u>glioblastoma</u>, lower patient age, higher <u>Karnofsky performance</u> score, accessible <u>tumor</u> location for <u>surgery</u>

* Negative prognostic factors: large <u>tumor</u> size (> 5–6 cm), midline-crossing tumors

### Brainstem glioma [[38]](/library/a3YQSK)




* Description: a <u>tumor</u> arising from the <u>glial cells</u> in the <u>brainstem</u> that may be low-grade (I-II) or high-grade (III-IV)

* <u>Epidemiology</u>: peak age 3–10 years

* Clinical features

* <u>Vomiting</u>

* <u>Cranial nerve</u> deficits

* <u>Ataxia</u>

* <u>Hydrocephalus</u>

* <u>Upper motor neuron signs</u>

* Diagnostics: <u>MRI</u>

* No <u>contrast enhancement</u>

* T2 <u>hyperintense</u> lesion

* Treatment

* Radiation and/or <u>chemotherapy</u>

* Surgical resection is often impossible

* Prognosis

* Poor, especially in diffuse <u>pontine gliomas</u>

* Median survival: ∼ 10 months

---

## Oligodendroglioma

* Description: : a <u>tumor</u> that arises from <u>oligodendrocytes</u>

* <u>Epidemiology</u>

* Median age: 40–50 years

* Relatively rare: ∼ 10% of primary <u>CNS</u> tumors

* Clinical features: : the most common location is the cerebral hemisphere (typically the <u>frontal lobe</u>) → <u>seizures</u>, <u>focal neurological deficits</u>, <u>personality</u> changes

* Diagnostics

* Imaging: intra-<u>parenchymal</u> <u>tumor</u> with calcifications [[39]](/library/foXkY_)

* CT: <u>hypodense</u> lesion

* <u>MRI</u>

* T1: <u>hypointense</u> or mixed lesions

* T2: <u>hyperintense</u> lesions

* <u>Biopsy</u> [[40]](/library/gjYF-K)

* Cells with a clear <u>cytoplasm</u> and round <u>nucleus</u> (<u>fried egg cells</u>)

* Chicken-wire pattern of <u>capillary</u> <u>anastomoses</u>

* Molecular testing: assessment of 1p/19q codeletion [[41]](/library/eoXxa_)

* Treatment

* Resection

* <u>Adjuvant radiotherapy</u> and <u>chemotherapy</u>

* Common chemotherapeutic regimens [[42]](/library/Ao1Re30)

* <u>Procarbazine</u> PLUS <u>lomustine</u> PLUS <u>vincristine</u>

* <u>Temozolomide</u> monotherapy

* Prognosis

* Recurrence rate ∼ 100%

* 5-year survival rate 50–60%

## Ependymoma

* Description: a <u>tumor</u> that arises from <u>ependymal cells</u> of the <u>ventricular system</u>

* <u>Epidemiology</u>: peak <u>incidence</u> in children and young adults

* Associated conditions: <u>neurofibromatosis type II</u>

* Clinical features: the <u>4<sup>th</sup> ventricle</u> is the most common location in children → <u>noncommunicating hydrocephalus</u> → <u>features of increased intracranial pressure</u> (e.g., <u>papilledema</u>, <u>headache</u>)

* Diagnostics

* Imaging: intra-<u>parenchymal</u> <u>tumor</u> with calcifications and cystic components due to <u>necrosis</u> and/or hemorrhage

* <u>Biopsy</u>

* Perivascular pseudorosettes

* Rod-shaped bodies (blepharoplasts) near the <u>nucleus</u>

* Treatment

* Resection

* <u>Adjuvant radiotherapy</u>

* Prognosis

* Depends on the WHO grade, but usually poor

* Overall 5-year survival rate: 65–90% [[43]](/library/boXH0_)[[44]](/library/XoX90_)

## Medulloblastoma

* Description: a highly <u>malignant tumor</u> derived from primitive, <u>neuroectodermal</u> tissue [[45]](/library/3v0S-3)

* <u>Epidemiology</u>

* Peak <u>incidence</u>: 1<sup>st</sup> decade

* Most common malignant pediatric <u>brain</u> <u>tumor</u> (20–25% of all cases)

* Associated conditions: <u>Turcot syndrome</u>

* Clinical features [[46]](/library/TYa6oQ)

* The most common location is the <u>cerebellum</u> → <u>cerebellar defects</u> (e.g., broad-based gait)

* Most tumors arise within the <u>cerebellar vermis</u> (midline) → <u>truncal ataxia</u>

* Invasion or compression of the <u>4<sup>th</sup> ventricle</u> → <u>noncommunicating hydrocephalus</u> → features of <u>raised intracranial pressure</u> (e.g., <u>papilledema</u>, <u>vomiting</u>, <u>headache</u>)

* <u>Drop metastases</u> to the spinal cord are common → <u>paraplegia</u>

* Diagnostics [[47]](/library/Rv0l-3)

* Imaging: intraparenchymal contrast-enhancing mass [[48]](/library/0oXe0_)

* <u>CT scan</u>: <u>isodense</u> or <u>hyperdense</u> mass

* <u>MRI</u>

* T1: <u>hypointense</u> mass

* T2: <u>isointense</u> mass

* <u>Biopsy</u>: <u>anaplastic</u> small round blue cells;  that surround a central <u>neuropil</u> (<u>Homer-Wright rosettes</u>)  [[49]](/library/p30Ljf)

* Treatment [[50]](/library/EL18zh0)

* Resection

* <u>Adjuvant therapy</u>

* Children ≥ 3 years: <u>chemotherapy</u> and craniospinal <u>radiotherapy</u>

* Children < 3 years: <u>chemotherapy</u>

* Common <u>chemotherapeutic agents</u>: <u>vincristine</u>, <u>cisplatin</u>, <u>cyclophosphamide</u>, <u>lomustine</u> [[50]](/library/EL18zh0)

* Prognosis

* 5-year survival rate: 60–80% [[51]](/library/aoXQ0_)[[52]](/library/hj0cZT)

* Poor prognostic factors [[53]](/library/GRYBoK)

* Inadequate resection

* Presence of <u>drop metastases</u>

* <u>ERBB2</u> mutation

## Craniopharyngioma

* Description: a benign dysontogenetic <u>tumor</u> arising from a remnant of the <u>Rathke pouch</u> (ectodermal derivative)

* <u>Epidemiology</u>

* <u>Bimodal distribution</u>: 5–14 years; second peak at 50–75 years

* Most common childhood <u>supratentorial</u> <u>tumor</u>

* Clinical features: The <u>tumor</u> arises in the suprasellar region and can extend into the intrasellar region. [[54]](/library/TjY6-K)

* Compression of the <u>pituitary gland</u> due to intrasellar extension → <u>hypopituitarism</u>

* <u>Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism</u>

* <u>Failure to thrive</u>

* Central <u>diabetes insipidus</u>

* Compression of the ventromedial <u>hypothalamic</u> <u>nucleus</u> → <u>hyperphagia</u> and <u>obesity</u>

* Compression of the <u>infundibular stalk</u> → disconnection <u>hyperprolactinemia</u>

* Compression of the <u>optic chiasm</u> → <u>bitemporal hemianopsia</u>

* Compression of <u>interventricular foramina</u> and/or aqueduct → <u>obstructive hydrocephalus</u>

* Diagnostics [[55]](/library/lxav95)

* Imaging: suprasellar calcified cyst with a lobulated contour

* <u>Biopsy</u>: <u>cholesterol</u> crystals found in a motor oil-like fluid on gross examination

* Consider obtaining <u>diagnostics for hypopituitarism</u>.

* Histological variants

* Adamantinomatous (common)

* Reticular <u>epithelial</u> cells

* Frequently associated with calcifications

* Cysts and <u>keratin</u> <u>nodules</u>

* <u>Papillary</u>

* <u>Metaplastic</u> squamous cells

* Calcifications and cysts are rare.

* No <u>keratin</u> <u>nodules</u>

* Differential diagnoses

* <u>Pituitary adenoma</u>

* <u>Rathke cleft cyst</u>

* Treatment

* Resection

* <u>Adjuvant radiotherapy</u>

* <u>Treatment of hypopituitarism</u>

* Prognosis: generally good, with a 10-year survival rate of ∼ 90%; however, the recurrence rate is high [[56]](/library/coXaa_)[[57]](/library/1oX2a_)[[58]](/library/XEX98-)

## Pineal gland tumor

* Description: a <u>tumor</u> that forms in or near the <u>pineal gland</u> and includes pineocytomas, pineoblastomas, and pineal <u>germinomas</u>

* <u>Epidemiology</u>

* <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u>

* < 1% of all <u>CNS</u> tumors in adults

* Clinical features
* Compression of <u>dorsal</u> <u>midbrain</u> leads to:

* Compression of <u>tectum</u> → <u>vertical gaze palsy</u> (<u>Parinaud syndrome</u>)

* Compression of <u>cerebral aqueduct</u> → <u>noncommunicating hydrocephalus</u>

* Compression of <u>hypothalamic</u> inhibiting pathways → increased <u>hCG</u> secretion → <u>precocious puberty</u>

* Diagnostics: <u>MRI</u> of the <u>brain</u> and <u>biopsy</u>

* <u>Histology</u>

* Approx. 70% are <u>germinomas</u> (similar appearance to <u>testicular seminoma</u>)

* Large vacuolated cells with round <u>nuclei</u> (<u>fried egg cells</u>)

* Lymphoid stroma

* Treatment

* Resection

* Adjuvant <u>radiochemotherapy</u>

---

## Hemangioblastoma

* Description: : a benign, highly vascularized <u>neoplasm</u>

* <u>Epidemiology</u>

* Rare

* Peak <u>incidence</u>: 20–50 years

* Associated conditions: <u>von Hippel-Lindau disease</u>

* Clinical features

* The <u>cerebellum</u> is the most common location → <u>cerebellar defects</u>

* Compression of the <u>4<sup>th</sup> ventricle</u> → <u>non-communicating hydrocephalus</u> → <u>features of raised ICP</u> (e.g., <u>papilledema</u>, <u>headache</u>)

* <u>Erythropoietin</u> production by <u>tumor</u> cells → secondary <u>polycythemia</u>

* Diagnostics

* <u>MRI</u>; : sharply demarcated intra-<u>parenchymal</u> cystic mass with a non-enhancing wall and an enhancing mural <u>nodule</u> in ∼ 60% of cases  [[59]](/library/WoXPa_)[[60]](/library/doXoa_)

* T2: <u>hyperintense</u> mass

* T1: <u>hypointense</u> or <u>isointense</u> mass

* <u>Biopsy</u>: thin-walled <u>capillary</u> vessels, densely packed together with scarce <u>parenchyma</u>

* Treatment

* Resection

* Antiangiogenic therapy (e.g., <u>bevacizumab</u>)

* Prognosis: Recurrence risk is < 20% in sporadic cases.  [[61]](/library/VoXGa_)

## Primary brain tumors according to age

### Pediatric primary brain tumors [[64]](/library/U30b3f)[[65]](/library/hJ1cF30)[[66]](/library/jJ1_F30)




* Most <u>pediatric brain tumors</u> are primary.

* Most common type of benign <u>pediatric primary brain tumor</u>: <u>pilocytic astrocytoma</u>

* Most common malignant <u>pediatric primary brain tumor</u>: <u>medulloblastoma</u>

* <u>Brain</u> tumors are the second most common cause of pediatric cancer;  after <u>leukemia</u>, accounting for approx. 20% of all cases of pediatric cancer and the primary cause of pediatric cancer deaths in the US.





| <br>Overview of <u>pediatric primary brain tumors</u> [[47]](/library/Rv0l-3)[[66]](/library/jJ1_F30)[[67]](/library/TF06h3)<br> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <u>Tumor</u> | Precursor | <br>Typical location  [[45]](/library/3v0S-3)<br> | <br>Typical <u>histology</u> [[49]](/library/p30Ljf)[[68]](/library/gJ1Ft30)<br> |
| <u>Supratentorial</u> |  |  |  |
| <br><u>Craniopharyngioma</u> [[55]](/library/lxav95)<br> | <br>* <u>Rathke pouch</u> (<u>ectoderm</u>)<br><br> | <br>* Suprasellar region<br><br> | <br><br>* Nests of <u>stratified</u> <u>squamous epithelium</u> with internal areas of lamellar <u>keratin</u> deposits<br><br>* <u>Cholesterol</u> crystals<br><br><br> |
| <u>Infratentorial</u> |  |  |  |
| <u>Pinealoma</u> | <br>* <u>Pineal gland</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Dorsal</u> <u>midbrain</u> (compression of <u>tectum</u>, <u>cerebral aqueduct</u>, and <u>hypothalamic</u> inhibiting pathways)<br><br> | <br><br>* Large vacuolated cells with round <u>nuclei</u> (<u>fried egg cells</u>)<br><br>* Lymphoid stroma<br><br>* Similar to <u>germ cell tumors</u> such as <u>testicular seminoma</u><br><br><br> |
| <br><u>Pilocytic astrocytoma</u><br> | <br>* <u>Astrocytes</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Posterior cranial fossa</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Rosenthal fibers: eosinophilic fibers with corkscrew-like configuration<br><br>* <u>GFAP</u> positive<br><br><br> |
| <u>Medulloblastoma</u> | <br>* Primitive, <u>neuroectodermal</u> tissue<br><br> | <br>* <u>Cerebellar vermis</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Small, round blue cells<br><br>* <u>Homer-Wright rosette</u><br><br>* <u>Synaptophysin</u> positive<br><br><br> |
| <br><u>Ependymoma</u> [[69]](/library/lv0vZR)<br> | <br>* <u>Ependymal cells</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>4<sup>th</sup> ventricle</u><br><br> | <br>* Perivascular pseudorosettes: <u>tumor</u> cells that are arranged in a <u>papillary</u> structure around a central blood vessel<br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> In children, most primary <u>brain</u> tumors arise <u>infratentorial</u>, <u>craniopharyngiomas</u> being an important exception.

### Adult primary brain tumors [[2]](/library/OL1IBh0)




* Primary <u>brain</u> tumors are less common than <u>brain metastases</u> in adults.

* Most common benign primary <u>brain</u> <u>tumor</u> in adults: <u>meningioma</u>

* Most common malignant primary <u>brain</u> <u>tumor</u> in adults: <u>glioblastoma multiforme</u>

* Primary <u>brain</u> tumors account for 1–2% of cancer cases in adults.





| <br>Overview of <u>adult primary brain tumors</u> [[47]](/library/Rv0l-3)[[67]](/library/TF06h3)<br> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <u>Tumor</u> | Precursor | <br>Typical locations [[45]](/library/3v0S-3)<br> | <br>Typical <u>histology</u> [[49]](/library/p30Ljf)<br> |
| <br><u>Glioblastoma multiforme</u> (WHO grade IV <u>astrocytoma</u>) [[70]](/library/5J1iu30)<br> | <br>* <u>Glial cells</u> (e.g., <u>astrocytes</u>)<br><br> | <br>* Cerebral hemispheres (<u>supratentorial</u>) <br>* May cross the corpus callosum (<u>butterfly glioma</u>)<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Pleomorphic</u> <u>anaplastic</u> cells that form <u>pseudopalisades</u> due to central <u>necrosis</u> or hemorrhage<br><br>* <u>Microvascular</u> <u>proliferation</u><br><br>* <u>GFAP</u> positive<br><br><br> |
| <br><u>Meningioma</u> [[71]](/library/MJ1Mu30)<br> | <br>* Arachnoid cap cells<br><br> | <br>* Extra-<u>parenchymal</u> <u>tumor</u> that can occur in <u>supratentorial</u> (often parasagittal) or <u>infratentorial</u> regions<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Spindle cells</u> arranged in whorls<br><br>* <u>Psammoma bodies</u><br><br><br> |
| <br><u>Hemangioblastoma</u> [[72]](/library/nJ17u30)<br> | <br>* Vascular system origin<br><br> | <br>* <u>Cerebellum</u> (<u>infratentorial</u>)<br><br> | <br>* Densely packed thin-walled <u>capillaries</u><br><br> |
| <br><u>Schwannoma</u> [[73]](/library/QjXuZy)<br> | <br>* <u>Schwann cells</u><br><br> | <br>* Cerebellopontine angle (<u>infratentorial</u>)<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Spindle cells</u> in palisades (Antoni A tissue) alternating with myxoid areas (Antoni B tissue)<br><br>* <u>S-100</u> positive<br><br><br> |
| <br><u>Oligodendroglioma</u> [[41]](/library/eoXxa_)<br> | <br>* <u>Oligodendrocytes</u><br><br> | <br>* Frontal lobes (<u>supratentorial</u>)<br><br> | <br><br>* Large vacuolated cells with round <u>nuclei</u> (<u>fried egg cells</u>)<br><br>* Chicken-wire pattern of <u>capillary</u> <u>anastomoses</u><br><br><br> |
| <br><u>Pituitary adenoma</u> [[74]](/library/OxaI95)<br> | <br>* <u>Pituitary</u> adenotrophic cells (typically <u>lactotrophs</u>)<br><br> | <br>* <u>Sella turcica</u> (<u>supratentorial</u>)<br><br> | <br>* Monomorphic, acidophilic or <u>basophilic</u>, polygonal cells arranged in sheets or cords<br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> In adults, most primary <u>brain</u> tumors arise <u>supratentorially</u>, <u>hemangioblastomas</u> and schwannomas being important exceptions.

## Brain metastases

### Definition




<u>Brain metastases</u> are secondary <u>brain</u> tumors due to <u>metastasis</u> of primary malignancies of other organs.




### <u>Epidemiology</u>




* Most common cause of <u>brain</u> tumors in adults [[11]](/library/9K1Ni30)

* Rare in children < 14 years of age [[75]](/library/0u1epi0)





### Etiology [[76]](/library/881Ooi0)




* <u>Lung cancer</u> (most common) [[76]](/library/881Ooi0)

* <u>Breast cancer</u>

* <u>Pancreatic cancer</u>

* <u>Malignant melanoma</u>

* <u>Renal cell carcinoma</u>

* <u>Colorectal carcinoma</u>

* <u>Testicular cancer</u> [[77]](/library/Zu1Zpi0)





### Clinical features




* Onset: acute or subacute due to rapid <u>tumor</u> growth

* <u>Seizures</u>

* <u>Focal neurological deficits</u>

* Cognitive deficits

* <u>Headaches</u>





### Diagnostics [[2]](/library/OL1IBh0)




* <u>Gadolinium</u>-enhanced <u>MRI</u>

* Well-circumscribed tumors at the junction of gray and <u>white matter</u> and/or <u>watershed areas</u> of the arterial system   [[78]](/library/SjYy-K)

* Small <u>metastases</u>: homogeneous <u>enhancement</u>

* Large <u>metastases</u>: <u>ring enhancement</u> due to central <u>necrosis</u>

* Further evaluation

* If the primary <u>tumor</u> is unknown: Obtain “<u>Diagnostics of cancer of unknown primary</u>.”

* If no primary <u>tumor</u> is identified: Obtain <u>biopsy</u> of the <u>brain metastasis</u>. [[4]](/library/To16Y30)





![Brain metastases in lung cancer](media/mifyfobd07uu4gqpdffcbcc7.jpg)

![Cerebral metastasis in lung carcinoma 1/2](media/wf4ryph9og1zms46cgljg0fx.jpg)

Cerebral metastasis in lung carcinoma 2/2




### Treatment [[4]](/library/To16Y30)[[79]](/library/So1yY30)




Management of <u>brain metastases</u> is based on the primary <u>tumor</u> type, extent of <u>metastases</u>, and the patient's <u>performance status</u>.




* <u>Anticancer therapies</u>: typically involves a combination of systemic and local therapy

* Systemic therapy: <u>chemotherapy</u>, <u>cancer immunotherapy</u>, and/or targeted agents

* Local therapy: radiosurgery, <u>radiation therapy</u>, and/or surgical resection

* Limited <u>brain metastases</u>: surgical resection or stereotactic radiosurgery (e.g., Gamma Knife, CyberKnife, proton beam)

* Extensive <u>brain metastases</u>: <u>stereotactic radiosurgery</u> and/or <u>whole-brain radiotherapy</u> (<u>WBRT</u>)

* Tumors causing <u>mass effect</u>: Consider surgical resection.

* <u>Supportive care</u>

* <u>Glucocorticoids</u>;  (e.g., <u>dexamethasone</u>) as needed to reduce <u>tumor</u> <u>edema</u> and <u>ICP</u> [[80]](/library/3abS4H)

* <u>Palliative care</u> for patients with a high primary <u>tumor</u> burden and a poor functional status (based on <u>Karnofsky performance status</u>)





### Prognosis [[81]](/library/xK1Ei30)




* Varies widely based on primary <u>tumor</u> and patient factors

* The <u>brain metastases</u> prognostic index  estimates survival in patients with <u>brain metastases</u>.
